Gull Harbor is a small town by the sea. There is an old lighthouse on the hill, and next to it there is a little radio station. You are the new volunteer. Nora is the host of the night program. She is tall and very friendly. Kofi is the technician. He is quiet, but he is really funny.
Hi! Are you the new volunteer?

The studio is small and messy. There are old records on the shelves and there are three microphones on the desk. Under the desk there is a strange wooden box. Nora is confused. "That box isn't mine. And it isn't Kofi's!"

Inside the box there is an old photo. In the photo there is a man with a white beard and a big black dog. The man's eyes are kind. The lighthouse is behind them. On the back of the photo there are three words: "Listen at midnight." Kofi is surprised. "Who is he?"

Nora works at the station five nights a week. She usually starts at six and finishes at eleven thirty. But tonight she isn't going home. She and Kofi are drinking hot chocolate and they are watching the clock. It's a quarter to twelve.

At midnight the radio makes a strange noise. Then a soft voice starts to read numbers: "Seven… fourteen… thirty… forty-one." Kofi is writing the numbers in his notebook. Nora isn't saying anything. She's listening very carefully. After two minutes, the voice stops.

The next morning, you show the photo to people in the town. A woman at the bakery knows the man. "That's Elias," she says. "He lives in the blue house near the port. He doesn't talk much, but he feeds the seagulls every morning at seven."

Elias invites you into his house. "Would you like some tea?" he asks. There isn't much furniture, but there are a lot of books and maps. "I was the lighthouse keeper for forty years," he says. "I was happy there. I could see the whole sea from the top."

"In October 1985 there was a terrible storm," Elias says. "A fishing boat was near the rocks, and the crew couldn't see the lights of the port. The lighthouse radio didn't work. But I had a small transmitter at home. I sent them numbers all night: the safe positions between the rocks. At six in the morning the boat arrived. Nobody died."

"But the signal is back," Nora says. "Did you send it?" Elias shakes his head. "No, I didn't. I can't use the transmitter now. My hands aren't strong anymore." That afternoon, Kofi goes to the lighthouse. He finds some new cables on the floor. There isn't any dust on them. Someone was there last night.

At midnight you hide in the lighthouse with Nora and Kofi. A young woman comes in with a laptop. It's Sara, Elias's granddaughter. "Please don't tell him," she says. "I found his old notebook last month. I wanted to finish his project. The numbers are a map of the sea for the fishermen." Sara is younger than Nora, but she knows more about radios than anyone in town.

Nora has an idea. "Next Saturday we're going to do a special program. Sara will explain the numbers, and I'll interview Elias. The whole town is going to listen." Then she gives instructions: "Kofi, check the antenna, please. Sara, bring your laptop. And you, call the fishermen and invite them. Don't forget!"

On Saturday the studio is full. Elias tells the story of the storm, and Sara explains the new sea map. Many fishermen call the station to thank them. It is the most popular program in the history of Gull Harbor. At the end, Elias looks at you and smiles. "Thank you," he says. "You gave my voice back to me."
